content: The recommendations were evaluated based on their applicability and feasibility. This evaluation was informed by the expertise and insights of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) members, as well as empirical and qualitative judgments derived from the evidence base used in the systematic review. Decisions within the GDG were made by consensus whenever possible. In cases of disagreement, final decisions were determined through voting criteria pre-approved by the WHO Guideline Review Committee (GRC). The voting criteria required a simple majority for weak or conditional recommendations and more than 70% agreement for strong recommendations. According to the GRADE approach, recommendations were categorized as either strong or weak and as being in favor of or against the intervention. WHO strongly recommends basic swim skills and water safety training programs for children aged six years or older in high-, low-, and middle-income countries. This recommendation is supported by moderate certainty in the evidence. The evidence summary for various types of basic swim skills and water safety training covered in the systematic review is presented. Additional evidence not used for this guideline is summarized in Annex 5. Basic swimming skill education programs may have little to no effect on certain swim skills while potentially improving others, but the evidence is highly uncertain (very low-certainty evidence). The effects on crude mortality rates by age group are also uncertain. Water safety training conducted out of water as part of broader educational programs will be addressed in a separate systematic review by the evidence synthesis team. Drowning is a significant and under-addressed cause of mortality, particularly affecting children and those in lowand middle-income countries. In high-income countries, basic swim skills and water safety training programs have been widely implemented to teach drowning prevention skills, knowledge, and behaviors to children, aiming to reduce fatal and nonfatal drowning incidents. The evidence supports the early implementation of training programs for children, suggesting improved mortality and morbidity outcomes with both basic swim skills and water safety training programs. Notably, the 15 studies analyzed indicated that earlier participation in training interventions by school-aged children may yield greater benefits, particularly in terms of appropriate water safety behaviors and knowledge. This may be due to providing proper education on the topic before children form their own opinions on how to act and stay safe in and around water, which could later be influenced by other factors. A few studies identified potential harms associated with training programs, including increased risk tolerance due to perceived skills and safety, parental perceptions that children require less supervision after training, general hazards associated with aquatic environments (e.g., drowning or injury during training), and the potential spread of communicable diseases. The GDG considered these concerns, noting that increased risk tolerance is common to many public health interventions. By recommending training that includes both swim skills and knowledge of water-safe behaviors, the undesirable effects were deemed to be minimal. The systematic review demonstrated a significant reduction in drowning-related mortality, a critical outcome, based on evidence of moderate certainty. While the review also uncovered outcomes (typically with lower certainty ratings) that inform knowledge and other swim-specific outcomes, these were considered interesting but less directly relevant to the critical outcome of drowning-related mortality. The critical outcome of drowning-related mortality was informed by a large non-randomized study that demonstrated a substantial effect size and was therefore deemed to be of moderate certainty for that outcome. After considering all other criteria within the Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) framework, the majority of the GDG concluded that the desirable effects of the intervention greatly outweigh the undesirable effects. Additionally, all other considerations, including cost-effectiveness, feasibility, acceptability, and equity, aligned in support of a strong favorable recommendation. The full rationale is presented in Annex 1, which also shows that the GDG acknowledged the limited and less robust evidence for harms, which did not dissuade them from issuing a strong recommendation. The GRADE tables for basic swim skills and water safety are presented in Annex 3. The relative success of training programs in high-income countries is partly attributed to regulatory frameworks developed through close collaboration between governments, public health entities, and stakeholders. The GDG emphasized that any recommendation for implementing swim skills and water safety training programs must include measures to ensure a safe environment for participants. Risk management approaches and regulations should include strategies to ensure the safety of participants and instructors, prevent communicable disease transmission, and provide acceptable, safe content and instructional techniques. Specific strategies for developing and implementing programs that impart swim skills and water safety knowledge are beyond the scope of this guideline but will be addressed in a derivative implementation guidance document from WHO. The GDG recognized that the resources required to initiate training programs vary depending on location, local knowledge, and existing infrastructure. The Bangladesh SwimSafe project demonstrated that effective and safe implementation of swim skills and water safety training could be achieved at a relatively low cost per child. The GDG encourages other programs to collect data and publish findings in peer-reviewed literature to enhance understanding of the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of this intervention. The GDG acknowledged that much of the evidence for this recommendation comes from observational and retrospective data. This dataset cannot establish a definitive causal relationship between swim skills and/or water safety training and drowning reduction, as other confounding factors may play a role. For example, swim skills training for children may also heighten caregivers’ awareness of the risks of unsupervised water activities, leading to observed decreases in drowning rates. Another limitation is the reliance on indirect evidence, where swimming skill performance and knowledge about safe behaviors are considered surrogates for individuals’ ability to protect themselves from drowning. WHO also strongly recommends day-care for children under six years of age as a drowning prevention strategy in countries with a high burden of drowning. This recommendation is supported by moderate certainty in the evidence. Formal day-care was shown to result in a statistically significant reduction in the risk of drowning-related deaths, injury-related deaths, and overall mortality compared to children not enrolled in a crèche program. Desirable effects were also found for child cognitive ability, academic achievement, mental health, and behavioral outcomes. However, inconsistent effects were noted for nutrition, obesity, and healthy behavior, while undesirable effects were related to infectious diseases, asthma, and psychological stress. Drowning is a leading cause of death among children under six years, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. A lack of capable supervision is a major risk factor for child drowning. Institutional supervision through formalized day-care arrangements within communities can reduce drowning deaths. The rationale for formalized day-care as a drowning prevention intervention is that it ensures constant adult supervision of beneficiary children. In settings where other modalities exist to ensure constant adult supervision, formalized day-care may not be strictly necessary as a drowning prevention intervention, though its additional desirable effects should not be overlooked. The panel noted that quality day-care programs improve family income by enabling women to enter the workforce while their children receive basic health, nutrition, and social and cognitive development in a nurturing and protective environment. Day-care programs also produce savings by improving the efficiency of educational systems through reductions in dropout rates, grade repetition, and remedial programs. Examples from Thailand and Vietnam show that national day-care and pre-school programs have been associated with decreased early childhood drowning rates. The GDG discussed the acceptability and sustainability of day-care programs in lowand middle-income countries. Parents are generally eager to improve their children’s educational opportunities and are willing to pay for high-quality day-care arrangements on a sliding scale or in-kind basis. Substantial government subsidies can make day-care interventions more acceptable. Child-care programs have greater benefits for children from high-risk home environments. Children, particularly girls, enrolled in child-care programs are more likely to enroll in primary school on time, improving their progress and performance. This also relieves child-care pressure on older siblings, enabling them to stay in school. Child-care programs support working women by providing safe environments for children and increasing family income. Programs with parental support can promote positive parenting and reduce the potential for violence, abuse, and neglect. Early childhood programs should be of high developmental quality, address child protection and safety, and ideally link to health and nutritional services to provide comprehensive child development services. Private or NGO-run programs must meet government-established educational, safety, and health standards. Implementation should also consider within-country inequities.
